n:
*Translator's note:* Or “righteousness” (KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV); NAB “justice”; NLT “hope for deliverance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the excavation of the hole.”

*Study note:* The “rock” and “quarry” refer here to Abraham and Sarah, the progenitors of the nation.

*Study note:* Although Abraham and Sarah are distant ancestors of the people the prophet is addressing, they are spoken of as the immediate parents.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one”; NLT “was alone”; TEV “was childless.”

*Translator's note:* “Bless” may here carry the sense of “endue with potency, reproductive power.” See {{Genesis 1:28|Gen 1:28}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I made him numerous.”

*Study note:* The rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) is known for its dry, desert-like conditions in the area of the Dead Sea and southward (although it also includes the Jordan Valley to the north). The wilderness (מִדְבָּר, midbar) is an area that receives less than twelve inches of rain per year and so can only support meager vegetation at best. The imagery here focuses on the transformation from arid and lifeless to watered and luxuriant.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “found in” (so NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* Or “certainly.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “instruction [or “a law”] will go out from me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my justice for a light to the nations I will cause to rest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my righteousness [or “vindication”] is near.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my deliverance goes forth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my arms will judge [on behalf of] nations.”

*Translator's note:* Or “islands” (NIV); TEV “Distant lands.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for my arm” (so NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will be torn in pieces.” The perfect indicates the certitude of the event, from the Lord’s rhetorical perspective.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my deliverance.” The same Hebrew word can also be translated “salvation” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT); cf. CEV “victory.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my righteousness [or “vindication”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will not be shattered [or “dismayed”].”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “people (who have) my law in their heart.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my vindication”; many English versions “my righteousness”; NRSV, TEV “my deliverance”; CEV “my victory.”

*Translator's note:* The arm of the Lord is a symbol of divine military power. Here it is personified and told to arouse itself from sleep and prepare for action.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Are you not the one who smashed?” The feminine singular forms agree grammatically with the feminine noun “arm.” The Hebrew text hasהַמַּחְצֶבֶת (hammakhtsevet), from the verbal root חָצַב (khatsav, “hew, chop”). The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has, probably correctly, המחצת, from the verbal root מָחַץ (makhats, “smash”) which is used in {{Job 26:12|Job 26:12}} to describe God’s victory over “the Proud One.”

*Translator's note:* This title (רַהַב, rahav, “proud one”) is sometimes translated as a proper name: “Rahab” (cf. NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV). It is used here of a symbolic sea monster, known elsewhere in the Bible and in Ugaritic myth as Leviathan. This sea creature symbolizes the forces of chaos that seek to destroy the created order. In the Bible “the Proud One” opposes God’s creative work, but is defeated (see {{Job 26:12|Job 26:12}}; {{Psalm 89:10|Ps 89:10}}). Here the title refers to Pharaoh’s Egyptian army that opposed Israel at the Red Sea (see v. {{Isaiah 51:10|10}}, and note also {{Isaiah 30:7|Isa 30:7}} and {{Psalm 87:4|Ps 87:4}}, where the title is used of Egypt).

*Translator's note:* The words “did you not” are understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line). The rhetorical questions here and in v. {{Isaiah 51:10|10}} expect the answer, “Yes, you certainly did!”

*Translator's note:* Hebrew תַּנִּין (tannin) is another name for the symbolic sea monster. See the note at {{Isaiah 27:1|27:1}}. In this context the sea creature represents Egypt. See the note on the title “Proud One” earlier in this verse.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “Are you not the one who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made…?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the redeemed” (so ASV, NASB, NIV, NRSV); KJV “the ransomed.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[will be] on their head[s].” “Joy” may be likened here to a crown (cf. {{2 Samuel 1:10|2 Sam 1:10}}). The statement may also be an ironic twist on the idiom “earth/dust on the head” (cf. {{2 Samuel 1:2|2 Sam 1:2}}; {{2 Samuel 13:19|13:19}}; {{2 Samuel 15:32|15:32}}; {{Job 2:12|Job 2:12}}), referring to a mourning practice.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “overtake” (so NIV); NASB “they will obtain.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “grief and groaning will flee.”

*Text-critical note:* The plural suffix should probably be emended to the second masculine singular (which is used in v. {{Isaiah 51:13|13}}). The final mem (ם) is probably dittographic; note the mem at the beginning of the next word.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, and of the son of man who [as] grass is given up?” The feminine singular forms should probably be emended to the masculine singular (see v. {{Isaiah 51:13|13}}). They have probably been influenced by the construction אַתְּ־הִיא (ʾat-hiʾ) in vv. {{Isaiah 51:9|9-10}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and that you forget.”

*Translator's note:* Or “the heavens” (also in v. {{Isaiah 51:16|16}}). The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and that you tremble constantly all the day.”

*Translator's note:* The question anticipates the answer, “Ready to disappear!” See v. {{Isaiah 51:14|14}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who is stooped over” (under a burden).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the pit” (so KJV); ASV, NAB “die and go down into the pit”; NASB, NIV “dungeon”; NCV “prison.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will not lack his bread.”

*Translator's note:* The addressee (second masculine singular, as in vv. {{Isaiah 51:13|13}}, {{Isaiah 51:15|15}}) in this verse is unclear. The exiles are addressed in the immediately preceding verses (note the critical tone of vv. {{Isaiah 51:12|12-13}} and the reference to the exiles in v. {{Isaiah 51:14|14}}). However, it seems unlikely that they are addressed in v. {{Isaiah 51:16|16}}, for the addressee appears to be commissioned to tell Zion, who here represents the restored exiles, “you are my people.” The addressee is distinct from the exiles. The language of v. {{Isaiah 51:16|16a}} is reminiscent of {{Isaiah 49:2|49:2}} and {{Isaiah 50:4|50:4}}, where the Lord’s special servant says he is God’s spokesman and effective instrument. Perhaps the Lord, having spoken to the exiles in vv. {{Isaiah 51:1|1-15}}, now responds to this servant, who spoke just prior to this in {{Isaiah 50:4|50:4-11}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I place my words in your mouth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with the shadow of my hand.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has לִנְטֹעַ (lintoaʿ, “to plant”). Several scholars prefer to emend this form to לִנְטֹת (lintot) from נָטָה (natah, “to stretch out”); see v. {{Isaiah 51:13|13}}, as well as {{Isaiah 40:22|40:22}}; {{Isaiah 42:5|42:5}}; {{Isaiah 44:24|44:24}}; {{Isaiah 45:12|45:12}}; cf. NAB, NCV, NRSV. However, since the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa, LXX (and Aquila and Symmachus), and Vulgate support the MT reading, there is no need to emend the form. The interpretation is clear enough: Yahweh fixed the sky in its place.

*Translator's note:* The infinitives in v. {{Isaiah 51:16|16b}} are most naturally understood as indicating the purpose of the divine actions described in v. {{Isaiah 51:16|16a}}. The relationship of the third infinitive to the commission is clear enough—the Lord has made the addressee (his special servant?) his spokesman so that the latter might speak encouraging words to those in Zion. But how do the first two infinitives relate? The text seems to indicate that the Lord has commissioned the addressee so that the latter might create the universe! Perhaps creation imagery is employed metaphorically here to refer to the transformation that Jerusalem will experience (see {{Isaiah 65:17|65:17-18}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[you] who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his anger.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the goblet, the cup [that causes] staggering, you drank, you drained.”
*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has אֲנַחֲמֵךְ (ʾanakhamekh), a first person form, but the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa reads correctly יְנַחֲמֵךְ (yenakhamekh), a third person form.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “those who are full of the anger of the Lord, the shout [or “rebuke”] of your God.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Lord,” from אֲדוֹן (ʾadon).

*Translator's note:* Many translations say “pleads the cause of his people” (KJV, NRSV, ESV) or similarly (NASB, NIV). The verb רִיב (riv, “to contend, dispute, conduct a law suit”) normally conveys that notion with the cognate direct object רִיב (riv, “cause, dispute, legal case”), but that is lacking here. Instead “his people” are the direct object, an unusual construction. The verb רִיב typically uses a preposition to indicate whether the action is done for or against someone. The syntax here may reflect {{Isaiah 3:13|Isa 3:13}} where God is said to judge his people. There רִיב occurs without a direct object, but “his people” are supplied by parallelism in the second half of the line. The immediate context here is about the reversal of judgment, so referring to God as the one who judges his people but now takes his cup of judgement away would fit well.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the cup of [= that causes] staggering” (so ASV, NAB, NRSV); NASB “the cup of reeling.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the goblet of the cup of my anger.”
*Translator's note:* That is, to make them drink it.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Shake yourself free from the dirt.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has שְּׂבִי (shevi), which some understand as a feminine singular imperative from יָשַׁב (yashav, “sit”). The LXX, Vulgate, Syriac, and the Targum support the MT reading (the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa does indirectly). Some interpret this to mean “take your throne”: The Lord exhorts Jerusalem to get up from the dirt and sit, probably with the idea of sitting in a place of honor (J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* [NICOT], 2:361)(cf. NLT, NIV, TNIV, HCSB). However, the form likely needs to be emended to שְׁבִיָּה (sheviyyah, “captive”), which appears in the parallel line (cf. NASB, RSV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and now what [following the marginal reading (*Qere*)] to me here?”

*Translator's note:* The verb appears to be a Hiphil form from the root יָלַל (yalal, “howl”), perhaps here in the sense of “mock.” Some emend the form to יְהוֹלָלוֹ (yeholalo) and understand a Polel form of the root הָלַל meaning here “mock, taunt.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is apparently a Hitpolal form (with assimilated tav, ת) from the root נָאַץ (naʾats), but GKC 151-52 §55.*b* explains it as a mixed form, combining Pual and Hitpolel readings.

*Translator's note:* The verb is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in that day” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “How delightful on the mountains.”

*Translator's note:* Or “has become king.” When a new king was enthroned, his followers would give this shout. For other examples of this enthronement formula (Qal perfect third person masculine singular מָלַךְ [malakh], followed by the name of the king), see {{2 Samuel 15:10|2 Sam 15:10}}; {{1 Kings 1:11|1 Kgs 1:11}}, {{1 Kings 1:13|13}}, {{1 Kings 1:18|18}}; {{2 Kings 9:13|2 Kgs 9:13}}. The Lord is an eternal king, but here he is pictured as a victorious warrior who establishes his rule from Zion.

*Translator's note:* קוֹל (qol, “voice”) is used at the beginning of the verse as an interjection.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “eye in eye”; KJV, ASV “eye to eye”; NAB “directly, before their eyes.”
*Translator's note:* Or “redeems.” See the note at {{Isaiah 41:14|41:14}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lays bare”; NLT “will demonstrate.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his holy arm.” This is a metonymy for his power.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the remote regions,” which here stand for the extremities and everything in between.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the deliverance of our God.” “God” is a subjective genitive here.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the vessels of the Lord” (so KJV, NAB).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “or go in flight”; NAB “leave in headlong flight.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “act wisely,” which by metonymy means “succeed.”

*Translator's note:* This piling up of synonyms emphasizes the degree of the servant’s coming exaltation.

*Translator's note:* Some witnesses read “him,” which is more consistent with the context, where the servant is spoken about, not addressed. However, it is possible that the Lord briefly addresses the servant here. The present translation assumes the latter view and places the phrase in parentheses.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “such was the disfigurement.” The noun מִשְׁחַת (mishkhat) occurs only here. It may be derived from the verbal root שָׁחַת (shakhat, “be ruined”; see BDB 1007-8 s.v. שָׁחַת). The construct form appears here before a prepositional phrase (cf. GKC 421 §130.*a*).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from a man his appearance.” The preposition מִן (min) here carries the sense “away from,” i.e., “so as not to be.” See BDB 583 s.v.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his form from the sons of men.” The preposition מִן (min) here carries the sense “away from,” i.e., “so as not to be.”

*Translator's note:* This statement completes the sentence begun in v. {{Isaiah 52:14|14a}}. The introductory כֵּן (ken) answers to the introductory כַּאֲשֶׁר (kaʾasher) of v. {{Isaiah 52:14|14a}}. Verses {{Isaiah 52:14|14b-15a}} are parenthetical, explaining why many were horrified.

*Translator's note:* Traditionally the verb יַזֶּה (yazzeh, a Hiphil stem) has been understood as a causative of נָזָה (nazah, “spurt, spatter”) and translated “sprinkle.” In this case the passage pictures the servant as a priest who “sprinkles” (or spiritually cleanses) the nations. Though the verb נָזָה does occur in the Hiphil with the meaning “sprinkle,” the usual interpretation is problematic. In all other instances where the object or person sprinkled is indicated, the verb is combined with a preposition. This is not the case in {{Isaiah 52:15|Isaiah 52:15}}, unless one takes the following עָלָיו (ʿalayv, “on him”) with the preceding line. But then one would have to emend the verb to a plural, make the nations the subject of the verb “sprinkle,” and take the servant as the object. Consequently some interpreters doubt the cultic idea of “sprinkling” is present here. Some emend the text; others propose a homonymic root meaning “spring, leap,” which in the Hiphil could mean “cause to leap, startle” and would fit the parallelism of the verse nicely.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Because of him kings will shut their mouths,” i.e., be speechless.

*Translator's note:* The perfect has a hypothetical force in this rhetorical question. For another example, see {{Genesis 21:7|Gen 21:7}}.

*Study note:* The speaker shifts here from God to an unidentified group (note the first person plural pronouns throughout vv. {{Isaiah 53:1|1-6}}). The content of the speech suggests that the prophet speaks here as representative of the sinful nation Israel. The group acknowledges its sin and recognizes that the servant suffered on their behalf.

*Translator's note:* The first half of v. {{Isaiah 53:1|1}} is traditionally translated, “Who has believed our report?” or “Who has believed our message?” as if the group speaking is lamenting that no one will believe what they have to say. But that doesn’t seem to be the point in this context. Here the group speaking does not cast itself in the role of a preacher or evangelist. No, they are repentant sinners, who finally see the light. The phrase “our report” can mean (1) the report which we deliver, or (2) the report which was delivered to us. The latter fits better here, where the report is most naturally taken as the announcement that has just been made in {{Isaiah 52:13|52:13-15}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to whom” (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the arm of the Lord.” The “arm of the Lord” is a metaphor of military power; it pictures the Lord as a warrior who bares his arm, takes up his weapon, and crushes his enemies (cf. {{Isaiah 51:9|51:9-10}}; {{Isaiah 63:5|63:5-6}}). But Israel had not seen the Lord’s military power at work in the servant.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “before him.” Some suggest an emendation to “before us.” If the third singular suffix of the Hebrew text is retained, it probably refers to the Lord (see v. {{Isaiah 53:1|1b}}). For a defense of this reading, see R. Whybray, *{{Isaiah 40|Isaiah 40-66}}* (NCBC), 173-74.

*Study note:* The metaphor in this verse suggests insignificance.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that we might see him.” The vav conjunctive prefixed to the imperfect introduces a result clause here. See GKC 504-5 §166.*a*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that we should desire him.” The vav conjunctive prefixed to the imperfect introduces a result clause here. See GKC 504-5 §166.*a*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “lacking of men.” If the genitive is taken as specifying (“lacking with respect to men”), then the idea is that he lacked company because he was rejected by people. Another option is to take the genitive as indicating genus or larger class (i.e., “one lacking among men”). In this case one could translate, “he was a transient” (cf. the use of חָדֵל [khadel] in Ps 39:5 HT [{{Psalm 39:4|39:4}} ET]).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a hiding of the face from him,” i.e., “like one before whom the face is hidden” (see BDB 712 s.v. מַסְתֵּר).

*Study note:* The servant is likened to a seriously ill person who is shunned by others because of his horrible disease.

*Study note:* Illness and pain stand by metonymy (or perhaps as metaphors) for sin and its effects, as vv. {{Isaiah 53:11|11-12}} make clear.

*Translator's note:* The words “for something he had done” are supplied in the translation for clarification. The group now realizes he suffered because of his identification with them, not simply because he was a special target of divine anger.

*Translator's note:* The preposition מִן (min) has a causal sense (translated “because of”) here and in the following clause.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the punishment of our peace [was] on him.” שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) is here a genitive of result, i.e., “punishment that resulted in our peace.”

*Study note:* Continuing to utilize the imagery of physical illness, the group acknowledges that the servant’s willingness to carry their illnesses (v. {{Isaiah 53:4|4}}) resulted in their being healed. Healing is a metaphor for forgiveness here.

*Translator's note:* Elsewhere the Hiphil of פָגַע (pagaʿ) means “to intercede verbally” (Jer 15:11; 36:25) or “to intervene militarily” ({{Isaiah 59:16|Isa 59:16}}), but neither nuance fits here. Apparently here the Hiphil is the causative of the normal Qal meaning, “encounter, meet, touch.” The Qal sometimes refers to a hostile encounter or attack; when used in this way the object is normally introduced by the preposition בְּ (bet, see {{Joshua 2:16|Josh 2:16}}; {{Judges 8:21|Judg 8:21}}; {{Judges 15:12|15:12}}, etc.). Here the causative Hiphil has a double object—the Lord makes “sin” attack “him” (note that the object attacked is introduced by the preposition בְּ. In their sin the group was like sheep who had wandered from God’s path. They were vulnerable to attack; the guilt of their sin was ready to attack and destroy them. But then the servant stepped in and took the full force of the attack.

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes the Niphal is passive; another option is take the clause (note the subject + verb pattern) as concessive and the Niphal as reflexive, “though he humbled himself.”

*Study note:* This verse emphasizes the servant’s silent submission. The comparison to a sheep does not necessarily suggest a sacrificial metaphor. Sheep were slaughtered for food as well as for sacrificial rituals, and טֶבַח (tevakh) need not refer to sacrificial slaughter (see {{Genesis 43:16|Gen 43:16}}; {{Proverbs 7:22|Prov 7:22}}; {{Proverbs 9:2|9:2}}; Jer 50:27; note also the use of the related verb in Exod 21:37 HT [{{Exodus 22:1|22:1}} ET]; {{Deuteronomy 28:31|Deut 28:31}}; {{1 Samuel 25:11|1 Sam 25:11}}).

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of this line is uncertain. The present translation assumes that מִן (min) here has an instrumental sense (“by, through”) and understands עֹצֶר וּמִמִּשְׁפָּט (ʿotser umimmishpat, “coercion and legal decision”) as a hendiadys meaning “coercive legal decision,” thus “an unjust trial.” Other interpretive options include: (1) “without [for this sense of מִן, see BDB 578 s.v. 1.b] hindrance and proper judicial process,” i.e., “unfairly and with no one to defend him,” (2) “from [in the sense of “after,” see BDB 581 s.v. 4.b] arrest and judgment.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and his generation, who considers?” (NASB similar). Some understand “his generation” as a reference to descendants. In this case the question would suggest that he will have none. However, אֶת (ʾet) may be taken here as specifying a new subject (see BDB 85 s.v. I אֵת 3). If “his generation” refers to the servant’s contemporary generation, one may then translate, “As for his contemporary generation, who took note?” The point would be that few were concerned about the harsh treatment he received.

*Study note:* The “land of the living” is an idiom for the sphere where people live, in contrast to the underworld realm of the dead. See, for example, {{Ezekiel 32:23|Ezek 32:23-27}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads “my people,” a reading followed by most English versions, but this is problematic in a context where the first person plural predominates, and where God does not appear to speak again until v. {{Isaiah 53:11|11b}}. Therefore, it is preferable to read with the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa עמו (“his people”). In this case, the group speaking in these verses is identified as the servant’s people (compare פְּשָׁעֵנוּ [peshaʿenu, “our rebellious deeds”] in v. {{Isaiah 53:5|5}} with פֶּשַׁע עַמִּי [peshaʿ ʿammi, “the rebellion of his people”] in v. {{Isaiah 53:8|8}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “one assigned his grave with criminals.” The subject of the singular is impersonal; English typically uses “they” in such constructions.

*Translator's note:* This line reads literally, “and with the rich in his death.” בְּמֹתָיו (bemotayv) combines a preposition, a plural form of the noun מוֹת (mot), and a third masculine singular suffix. The plural of the noun is problematic and the יו may be the result of virtual dittography. The form should probably be emended to בָּמָתוֹ (bamato, singular noun). The relationship between this line and the preceding one is uncertain. The parallelism appears to be synonymous (note “his grave” and “in his death”), but “criminals” and “the rich” hardly make a compatible pair in this context, for they would not be buried in the same kind of tomb. Some emend עָשִׁיר (ʿashir, “rich”) to עָשֵׂי רָע (ʿase raʿ, “doers of evil”) but the absence of the ayin (ע) is not readily explained in this graphic environment. Others suggest an emendation to שְׂעִירִים (seʿirim, “he-goats, demons”), but the meaning in this case is not entirely transparent and the proposal assumes that the form suffered from both transposition and the inexplicable loss of a final mem. Still others relate עָשִׁיר (ʿashir) to an alleged Arabic cognate meaning “mob.” See *HALOT* 896 s.v. עָשִׁיר. Perhaps the parallelism is antithetical, rather than synonymous. In this case, the point is made that the servant’s burial in a rich man’s tomb, in contrast to a criminal’s burial, was appropriate, for he had done nothing wrong.

*Translator's note:* If the second line is antithetical, then עַל (ʿal) is probably causal here, explaining why the servant was buried in a rich man’s tomb, rather than that of criminal. If the first two lines are synonymous, then עַל is probably concessive: “even though….”

*Study note:* What constitutes the servant’s reparation offering? Some might think his suffering, but the preceding context views this as past, while the verb here is imperfect in form. The offering appears to be something the servant does after his suffering has been completed. Perhaps the background of the language can be found in the Levitical code, where a healed leper would offer a reparation offering as part of the ritual to achieve ceremonial cleanliness (see Lev 14). The servant was pictured earlier in the song as being severely ill. This illness (a metaphor for the effects of the people’s sin) separated him from God. However, here we discover the separation is not final; once reparation is made, so to speak, he will again experience the Lord’s favor.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of this line is uncertain. It reads literally, “if you/she makes, a reparation offering, his life.” The verb תָּשִׂים (tasim) could be second masculine singular, in which case it would have to be addressed to the servant or to God. However, the servant is only addressed once in this servant song (see {{Isaiah 52:14|52:14a}}), and God either speaks or is spoken about in this servant song; he is never addressed. Furthermore, the idea of God himself making a reparation offering is odd. If the verb is taken as third feminine singular, then the feminine noun נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) at the end of the line is the likely subject.
